content: The HOTT program connects clients to preventive services that prioritize harm reduction strategies. To ensure a trans-affirming environment, all HOTT staff, including medical providers, nurses, case managers, and HIV test providers—many of whom identify as members of the LGBTQ+ community—are trained in transgender-competent service provision. Trans-inclusive program literature and health education materials are made available. Weekly support groups for transgender women, such as The Girls Room, provide a safe space for this often hard-to-reach population to explore and support their gender transition. Feedback on transgender services is gathered through a Youth Advisory Board, The Girls Room, and annual clinic-wide surveys. The Center of Excellence for Transgender Health aims to increase access to comprehensive, effective, and affirming healthcare services for transgender and gender-variant communities. Its ultimate goal is to improve the overall health and well-being of transgender individuals by developing and implementing programs that address community-identified needs. The Center's core faculty and staff, with diverse backgrounds and expertise, work alongside a national advisory board of 14 transgender leaders from across the United States. The Center addresses a wide range of health issues for transgender individuals, including primary and preventive care, hormone therapy, mental health, youth services, and surgical care. Additionally, the Transitions Project builds the capacity of community-based organizations to adapt, implement, and evaluate evidence-based HIV prevention interventions for transgender communities. The Transgender Family Program, established in 2004 at Community Healthcare Network clinics in New York City, improves access to HIV prevention and primary healthcare services. The program integrates transgender care, HIV testing and counseling, medical case management, treatment adherence support, STI screening and treatment, mental health services, nutritional services, and prevention interventions. It also provides risk reduction counseling, support groups, outreach, bilingual educational workshops, and referrals to legal and social services. Recruitment strategies include face-to-face contact, community-based activities, and online methods such as social media. Clients are encouraged to involve family members, which has proven effective in increasing access and attendance. Over 750 individuals have received transgender-specific services, with benefits including improved community tolerance, increased accessibility, flexible service hours, and access to a range of in-house support services. Evaluations have shown significant decreases in sex work, needle sharing, and unregulated hormone injections, along with increased condom use. Aksion Plus, founded in 1992, was the first youth NGO to address HIV through education and awareness-raising activities. It now supports health and human rights interventions in six cities for young people who inject drugs, young sex workers, and young LGBTQ+ individuals. Aksion Plus provides direct services and referrals for HIV and STI care, opioid substitution therapy, and harm reduction training for NGOs and government bodies. Outreach workers distribute needles, syringes, and condoms while providing counseling and referrals. Peer educators from key populations play a critical role in ensuring the success of interventions. The program also organizes workshops and events to share experiences and best practices. The Boysproject in Antwerp, Belgium, supports male and transgender sex workers by using social media to create demand for social and medical services, provide information, and offer referrals. It operates a weekly drop-in center with services from social workers and doctors, language courses, and a space for conversation and shared experiences. The project collaborates with the Institute of Tropical Medicine to provide HIV post-exposure prophylaxis and reached 298 sex workers in 2013. Social workers play a vital role in guiding individuals through the PEP process. The PASMO/PSI Combination Prevention Program in Central America increases access to HIV prevention interventions for key populations. It addresses high-risk behaviors, stigma, and discrimination while improving access to essential prevention and health services. The program provides a comprehensive package of behavioral, biomedical, and structural interventions, including behavior change communication, STI screening and treatment, and referrals to medical and structural services. It collaborates with Ministries of Health, NGOs, and private clinics to deliver services. Sensitization and training of healthcare providers and community mobilization are used to address hostility and discrimination. AFEW (AIDS Foundation East-West) works in Eastern Europe and Central Asia to reduce the impact of HIV on key populations. Through client management initiatives, AFEW strengthens local service provider networks and resources. Client managers assist individuals in assessing their needs and developing strategies to address them. Social workers and client managers, often from key populations, are trained in human rights and ethics. AFEW organizes workshops and events to share experiences and best practices. However, local residency permit requirements remain a barrier to accessing services, which NGOs like AFEW address through agreements with local providers. The Egyptian Family Planning Association (EFPA) uses outreach to engage at-risk youth with comprehensive, gender-sensitive, rights-based sexual and reproductive health education. Peer educators conduct outreach sessions with young people, including those in government institutions for street children and orphanages, to explain clinic services, encourage attendance, and distribute condoms. Outreach is also conducted with young key populations not connected to institutions, such as truck drivers. EFPA also advocates for policy changes to prioritize youth SRH needs within the national health system. The Pehchan program in India strengthens the capacity of community-based organizations (CBOs) to provide HIV prevention programming for men who have sex with men, transgender individuals, and hijras (MTH populations). It fosters community-friendly services, advocates for improved well-being, and complements the government’s HIV prevention strategy. The program involves MTH community members as managers and advisors, building trust and community ownership. Pehchan has developed Crisis Response Teams to address violence and initiated a national advocacy campaign for decriminalizing homosexuality. It also works to reduce HIV stigma within MTH communities through outreach and counseling. LVCT Health provides essential services for men who have sex with men and sex workers outside traditional settings to overcome barriers to care. Its peer-led approach involves community engagement to ensure consistent access to services.
